The buyer needs to understand dependence and develop credible commitments. A contract can support the relationship, but the quality of interaction and the availability of alternatives remain important.

A high-impact/high-risk situation can sometimes be changed. Redesign may allow more standard components. Supplier development may create another source. A change in technology may make the purchase less unique. Strategic management includes changing the situation where feasible, not only accepting the quadrant.

## Kraljic's four-stage process

[diagram:kraljicprocess]

### Stage 1: purchasing classification

Assess categories using profit impact and supply risk. Determine which purchases deserve which form of attention. The familiar two-by-two matrix belongs here. Classification should be based on the business situation and reviewed when conditions change.

### Stage 2: market analysis

Examine the strength and characteristics of the supply market and the buying company. Relevant considerations include supplier capacity and utilisation, cost structures, break-even conditions, uniqueness, entry barriers, demand growth, the buyer's volume and the consequences of non-delivery. The article uses a structured comparison rather than a vague impression of whether a supplier seems powerful.

A buyer large in its own market can still be a small customer for a global supplier. Conversely, a supplier with a unique product may depend heavily on one customer's volume. Relative position must be assessed for the relationship and requirement under discussion.

### Stage 3: strategic positioning

For significant purchases, compare the company's buying strength with the supply market's strength. Kraljic uses a further three-by-three portfolio analysis with broad directions to **exploit**, **balance** or **diversify**. This is a separate analysis from the first two-by-two matrix.

Where buying strength is high relative to supply-market strength, the firm can exploit its purchasing position carefully. In more balanced situations, it needs an appropriately balanced strategy. Where the supply market is stronger and dependence is high, diversification and reducing vulnerability become important.

Diversify does not necessarily mean splitting every current order equally tomorrow. The article notes that short-term concentration can sometimes help secure supply while the firm develops longer-term alternatives, substitutions or backward integration. Timing and feasibility matter.

### Stage 4: action plans

Translate the analysis into practical choices about volume, price, contracts, spot purchasing, new suppliers, stock, make-or-buy decisions, value engineering and logistics. Assign responsibility, timing and contingencies. A completed matrix without actions has not completed the strategic work.

For Campus Tees, an action plan might standardise office purchases, tender standard blanks among qualified sources, hold a buffer of a hard-to-source spare part, and schedule joint maintenance and capacity reviews with a critical equipment partner. Different purchases produce different actions because the risk and economic consequences differ.

## What makes an assessment credible?

Use evidence rather than only labels. For supply risk, ask how many suppliers are technically qualified, how quickly they can deliver, whether capacity is constrained and what it takes to switch. For profit impact, ask about spend, final-product performance, growth opportunities and the economic effects of failure.

The original article emphasises organisational capabilities too: data, skills, management attention and forecasting. Purchasing needs enough information to anticipate problems rather than react to each missing item. Central coordination may create bargaining strength, while local knowledge can improve decisions about specific needs.

A rolling forecast is useful only if it connects to action. If a buyer sends forecasts nobody believes, the apparent information sharing may not improve supply. The quality of collaboration and the credibility of commitments influence how suppliers respond.

## Strengths and limitations

The matrix is easy to communicate, helps prioritise scarce management time and connects purchasing decisions with different supply conditions. It discourages one-size-fits-all purchasing. It also creates a common language for discussing why some purchases need collaboration and others need simpler processing.

Its categories can oversimplify a changing network. The boundaries between high and low depend on judgment. A supplier may provide several categories of item. Relationships can create capabilities not visible in a simple spend-risk score. One buyer's attempt to reduce risk can transfer it upstream rather than reduce it for the whole chain.

The model also needs regular reassessment. A disruption can move a standard blank shirt from leverage toward a higher-risk category. A redesign may move a unique connector out of the bottleneck quadrant. Dynamic analysis is stronger than memorising a permanent list of products.

Use the matrix together with the network perspective. Kraljic helps differentiate purchasing priorities. ARA helps explain the relationships, resources and activities through which a strategy is actually implemented. A strategic partnership only creates value if those connections work.

### Check your understanding

A €2 component has only one qualified source, but spending on it is tiny. Is it routine because it is cheap?

[answer:Possible answer]
No. Low spending does not imply low supply risk. If the component has low overall profit impact but high supply risk, it is a bottleneck item and continuity measures are appropriate. If its effect on business performance makes profit impact high as well, it may be strategic. Explain the chosen assessment rather than deciding from price alone.
[/answer]


# Operations: turn resources into outcomes

Operations management concerns the transformation of inputs into useful outputs. In a factory, the transformation may physically alter materials. In a service organisation, it may change information, a customer's location or a customer's condition. The central question is how resources and activities create the outcome the customer needs.

Campus Tees transforms blank shirts, ink, design information, labour, equipment and management effort into finished event shirts and associated service. A printing machine matters, but so do the processes that obtain correct artwork, allocate capacity and check whether an order is complete.

## The transformation model

[diagram:transformation]

The lecture identifies inputs such as material, machines, labour, management and capital. A transformation process uses them to create goods and services. Feedback connects the result to future decisions. If customers report that prints fade after washing, that information should influence materials, methods, quality checks or specifications.

**In plain English:** something comes in, work changes it, something useful comes out, and information about the result helps improve the next attempt. Do not assume “transformation” always means cutting or assembling a physical object. An accountant transforms records into financial information; a delivery company changes where a parcel is located.

Inputs can constrain the output in different ways. Excellent materials do not compensate for an impossible schedule. Skilled employees cannot use an unavailable machine. Capital invested in excessive inventory can limit funds available for improvements. The model encourages you to consider the combined system rather than one isolated resource.

## Processes, subprocesses and activities

A process connects a customer need to a satisfied customer through linked work. A subprocess is a part of that larger process. An activity is a more specific task. The level of detail depends on the question you are analysing.

For Campus Tees, “fulfil a club order” is a process. “Prepare approved artwork” can be a subprocess. “Check the file resolution” is an activity within it. Inputs and outputs connect the tasks: the approved file becomes an input to production planning and printing.

This distinction helps when diagnosing a problem. If late delivery originates in artwork approval, improving only the physical printing speed may have little effect. The process view follows the customer's outcome across departments and handovers. A departmental chart alone may hide the waiting between them.

A good map shows the actual process rather than an ideal procedure that staff do not follow. It should expose queues, repeated checks, missing information and unclear responsibilities. The purpose is to improve understanding and decisions, not to produce the most complicated possible diagram.

## Read the process-map symbols

The lecture's SCM symbols include an information flow, a material flow, a supplier or customer, delivery, inventory, a process step and a data box. It also distinguishes a push arrow and the movement of finished goods to a customer.

| Symbol or element | What it tells you | Campus Tees interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Information-flow line | A message or instruction moves. | An approved design or order enters planning. |
| Material-flow arrow | Physical things move. | Blank shirts move to printing. |
| Supplier/customer icon | An external party connects to the process. | A wholesaler supplies the blanks. |
| Delivery/truck | Transport or shipment occurs. | Finished shirts leave with the carrier. |
| Inventory triangle | Stock waits at a point in the flow. | A pile of blanks awaits processing. |
| Process box | Work transforms or handles something. | Printing, inspection or packing occurs. |
| Data box | Relevant measurements describe the step. | Cycle time, resources or other process data. |

Symbols help you see relationships consistently. They are not the analysis itself. A triangle tells you that stock exists; it does not tell you whether that stock is wasteful, necessary for service or compensating for unreliable supply. Ask why it is present and what would happen if it were removed.

## Quality approaches: TQM, Kaizen, BPR and Six Sigma

**Total Quality Management (TQM)** is described in the course as an organisation-wide effort to work with quality and continuous improvement. Quality is not left only to a final inspector. Purchasing, design, production, administration and customer service all affect it.

**Kaizen** means continuous improvement. Staff repeatedly make and evaluate improvements to the way work is done. Campus Tees might introduce a clearer artwork checklist, then refine it after identifying recurring misunderstandings. Small changes can accumulate into a substantial improvement.

**Business Process Reengineering (BPR)** concerns radical redesign of core workflows and processes for dramatic improvements in productivity, cycle time and quality. Instead of adding one more signature to an inefficient process, the firm may redesign how the order is handled from beginning to end.

**Six Sigma** is a data-driven approach to reducing defects and variability. In our example, the team would measure printing errors, investigate causes and assess whether changes reduce the problem. Do not use Six Sigma as a generic word for every improvement effort.

| Approach | Central emphasis | Simple illustration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TQM | Organisation-wide responsibility for quality. | Sales, purchasing and printing jointly prevent incorrect orders. |
| Kaizen | Ongoing improvement. | Improve the order checklist every time a useful lesson appears. |
| BPR | Radical process redesign. | Replace several disconnected order forms with a redesigned end-to-end flow. |
| Six Sigma | Data, defects and variability. | Measure misprints and identify which conditions explain them. |

The glossary's statement that TQM is often replaced by ISO9000, Six Sigma and lean should be read as the source's broad teaching description. These ideas can coexist. Do not infer a universal rule that TQM has ceased to exist or that each later method has exactly the same purpose.

## The seven wastes: MUDA

The seven wastes in the lecture and glossary are overproduction, defects, inventory, motion, overprocessing, transporting and waiting. A practical answer defines each and shows what the unnecessary resource use looks like.

| Waste | Plain explanation | Campus Tees example | Improvement question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overproduction | Make more or earlier than needed. | Print 100 unapproved extra shirts. | What real demand authorises this output? |
| Defects | Work fails requirements and needs correction or disposal. | Print the wrong logo. | How can the error be prevented at its source? |
| Inventory | Resources sit unused or waiting. | Keep boxes of unpopular sizes for months. | Which uncertainty or timing mismatch creates this stock? |
| Motion | Unnecessary movement by people. | Walk repeatedly across the room for tools. | Can the layout or workplace organisation improve? |
| Overprocessing | Do more work than the requirement needs. | Enter the same order details into three disconnected forms. | Does the customer or process need this extra step? |
| Transporting | Unnecessary movement of goods. | Carry batches between distant rooms several times. | Can material flow become shorter and simpler? |
| Waiting | People, machines or goods cannot proceed. | A finished batch waits for an approval already given by email. | What dependency or missing information causes the delay? |

Motion concerns people; transport concerns goods. Overproduction creates unnecessary output; inventory is the stock that may result. They are related but not identical. A stock of essential spare parts may be intentional protection rather than something to remove without analysis.

Waste elimination should preserve the required outcome. Removing a necessary quality check before the underlying process is capable can increase defects. The better question is how to prevent the defect and make the check unnecessary, not how to cut every visible activity immediately.

## Time-based process mapping

[diagram:timeprocess]

A time-based map separates activity time from waiting or wasted time. The lecture's example shows long delays between relatively short operations. Its redesigned process reduces elapsed time by addressing the way work is organised, rather than simply making every processing task faster.

In a simple teaching example, an order takes 16 hours from entry to completion. Four hours involve useful activity and twelve hours are waiting. If the activity is made 25% faster, one hour is saved. If half the waiting is removed, six hours are saved. This explains why managers should examine queues and handovers, not only machine speed.

The lecture's original map runs to roughly 69 elapsed hours and the redesigned version to roughly 38. These are visual readings of the chart, not precision measurements. The redesign includes booking work at goods-in, operators picking up their own jobs, multiskilling and self-inspection. The basic operations remain broadly similar while organisation changes substantially.

Waiting can arise from batching, unavailable information, separate inspection queues, unclear ownership or priorities that conflict across functions. Improvements should target the cause. Telling employees to “work faster” will not resolve a missing approval or a job waiting in the wrong queue.

## Cause-and-effect analysis

[diagram:fishbone]

A cause-and-effect or fishbone diagram organises possible causes of a problem. The lecture groups possibilities under people, machines, material and methods. These categories help teams investigate systematically rather than jump to the first plausible explanation.

For late orders, people-related possibilities might include missing training or unclear responsibility. Machine-related possibilities might include breakdowns or long setups. Material-related possibilities might include shortages or unsuitable blanks. Method-related possibilities might include duplicate data entry or batch rules.

The diagram contains hypotheses. It does not prove that every listed cause is real. Evidence, observation and measurement are needed. A good answer makes that distinction: brainstorming a possible explanation is the start of diagnosis, not the end.

A problem can involve several causes at once. A machine failure may be more damaging because the schedule has no recovery capacity and the supplier lead time for a spare is long. This connects operations with purchasing, inventory and resilience. The module's concepts become more useful when you combine them around a concrete problem.

## Why reducing waste and time can reduce cost

The operations lecture highlights working capital, plant and equipment capital, development costs and quality costs. Faster flow can reduce money tied up in work-in-progress. Better use of capacity can reduce the need for extra equipment. Shorter development cycles can reduce delays and repeated work. Preventing defects can reduce scrap, correction and customer-service costs.

These effects are conditional. A faster process that produces the wrong variant earlier has not necessarily improved value. A reduction in inventory that creates repeated stoppages may raise total cost. The aim is a better flow of useful output toward customer needs.

### Check your understanding

Why might a 50% faster machine produce only a small improvement in customer lead time?

[answer:Possible answer]
If most lead time consists of waiting for artwork, materials, inspection or dispatch, the machine affects only a small part of the total. A time-based process map identifies where the elapsed time is actually spent. Improvements to handovers and queues may save more time than increasing processing speed alone.
[/answer]


# Lean, agile and leagile supply chains

Lean and agile are responses to different operating conditions. Lean emphasises waste elimination and stable flow. Agile emphasises responsiveness in volatile markets. Naylor, Naim and Berry show how they can be combined in one supply chain through a decoupling point. The word **leagility** names that combination.

The central design problem is timing. Some activities take longer than the customer is willing to wait. A business must decide what to prepare in advance, what to leave until an actual order arrives and where to hold stock or capacity. The answer affects cost, variety, speed and risk.

## P-time, D-time and the gap

**P-time** is the production lead time; the lecture's diagram follows source, make and deliver. **D-time** is the time the customer is willing to wait. If P-time is longer than D-time, the full process cannot begin only after receiving the customer order and still meet the promise.

[diagram:ptime]

Suppose obtaining blanks takes five days, printing takes two and delivery takes one. P-time is eight days. If a club will wait three days, Campus Tees needs some preparation in advance or a change to the process. It might hold blank shirts, shorten supply lead time, reserve capacity or offer a different promise.

The P-time minus D-time gap indicates the part that must be anticipated or otherwise bridged. Forecasting is one way to prepare, but postponement can reduce the detail that must be forecast. It is easier to prepare common blank shirts than to predict every club's final logo in advance.

Do not assume that all production should be forecast-driven or that all activities can wait for a firm order. The design depends on actual lead times and customer expectations. A unique engineered product may require a long accepted wait. A standard retail product may need immediate availability.

## The customer order decoupling point

The lecture defines the **CODP**, or customer order decoupling point, as “the point where the product is linked to a specific order”.

**In plain English:** before this point, the business is preparing something generic or based on expected demand. After this point, the work is connected to a particular customer's actual order. The point divides different information requirements and operating priorities.

Campus Tees may stock plain shirts and wait for confirmed artwork before printing. Its generic shirts are not yet assigned to one club. Printing links them to the specific order. If it instead stocked finished club designs, the decoupling point would be further downstream and demand would need to be predicted in more specific detail.

The CODP is not simply whichever physical warehouse appears in a drawing. It has an information meaning: where does a product become committed to a particular order? A stock point often supports that transition, but the conceptual distinction is the order linkage.

## Postponement

> “Postponement is a business strategy which maximizes possible benefit and minimizes risk by delaying further investment into a product or service until the last possible moment”.

**Source:** Operations lecture, slide 10.

**In plain English:** keep options open by delaying a decision or transformation that makes the product more specific, until better information is available. The objective is not to deliver late; it is to delay commitment while still meeting the customer's deadline.

[diagram:postpone]

For Campus Tees, buying generic white blanks before the event and printing confirmed designs later postpones differentiation. It reduces the risk of guessing the wrong design. It does not eliminate the need to predict total blank demand or the required size range.

The reading discusses examples such as delaying national configuration of printers. A common base can be held until the destination's needs are known, then configured appropriately. Benetton's delayed dyeing is another helpful illustration of postponing a colour decision until better demand information is available.

Postponement requires a suitable product and process. If final customisation takes longer than D-time, it cannot simply be moved after the order without changing something else. Modular design, reliable common components, flexible capacity and good information can make postponement feasible.

## Exact definitions: lean and agile

> “Leanness means developing a value stream to eliminate all waste, including time, and to ensure a level schedule.”

> “Agility means using market knowledge and a virtual corporation to exploit profitable opportunities in a volatile market place.”

**Source:** Naylor, Naim and Berry (1999), p. 108.

**Lean in plain English:** remove unnecessary work and delay, and make the flow stable and efficient. **Agile in plain English:** understand changing demand and use a flexible network of capabilities to respond profitably. Agility is more than rushing; it requires knowledge and the ability to reconfigure work.

A virtual corporation in this discussion concerns coordinated capabilities across organisations. It does not merely mean an online shop. The business can combine resources in a network without owning every activity, which connects the reading with purchasing and industrial networks.

## Compare the paradigms carefully

| Dimension | Lean emphasis | Agile emphasis | Shared concern |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Demand conditions | A reasonably level and predictable schedule helps. | Volatile demand requires flexibility. | Understanding the market. |
| Main competitive emphasis | Cost and efficient flow. | Service and responsiveness. | Quality and lead-time performance. |
| Waste elimination | Essential to the paradigm. | Desirable, while responsiveness remains central. | Avoid resources that add no useful value. |
| Reconfiguration | Useful, but stability supports the flow. | Rapid reconfiguration is essential. | Match capabilities to the task. |
| Buffers | Reduce unnecessary inventory and delay. | Some inventory or capacity may support response. | Use the minimum reasonable protection for the situation. |

The paper does not argue that one paradigm universally replaces the other. Many foundations are shared: market knowledge, integration and lead-time reduction. The difference concerns which attributes become essential for the operating conditions and order-winning requirements.

Lean does not mean “no inventory under any circumstances”. Agile does not mean “ignore costs”. Both should be economically sensible. A buffer or reserve capacity may be justified when it enables a profitable response to uncertainty. The paper's minimum reasonable inventory idea is more useful than blindly pursuing a literal zero.

## Leagility: combine the two

[diagram:leagile]

The standard leagile arrangement is **lean upstream, agile downstream**, with a decoupling point between them. Upstream, common work is planned and levelled where possible. Downstream, the business responds to actual customer orders and variety. A suitable stock point protects the responsive part from some upstream uncertainty.

Campus Tees buys common blanks efficiently in advance and then uses flexible printing to fulfil confirmed club designs. It avoids both extremes: attempting to source every input after a late order, or printing every possible club design for stock. Commonality supports efficiency; delayed differentiation supports responsiveness.

The combined system still needs coordination. If upstream supply is unreliable, downstream agility may be overwhelmed. If downstream printing capacity is insufficient, a stock of blanks does not guarantee fast delivery. Leagility is a design of connected activities, not a slogan attached to one warehouse.

## Five decoupling-point positions

| Position | What waits for the order? | What is prepared in advance? | Main implication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Buy to order | Procurement as well as making and delivery. | Very little product-specific stock. | High customisation can require a long customer wait. |
| Make to order | Manufacturing or transformation. | Raw materials or suitable inputs. | Less finished-stock risk, but production time remains after the order. |
| Assemble to order | Final assembly or configuration. | Common components or modules. | Faster response with fewer finished variants in stock. |
| Make to stock | Mainly allocation and delivery of finished goods. | Finished products based on forecasts. | Quick service but greater exposure to variant forecast errors. |
| Ship to stock | The customer selects from locally positioned stock. | Finished goods near the market. | Very short wait with more downstream stock commitments. |

Moving the point downstream usually reduces the customer's remaining wait while increasing advance commitment to specific products or locations. Moving it upstream preserves flexibility and reduces some finished-stock exposure while asking the customer to wait longer. The precise result depends on the product, process and logistics design.

An assemble-to-order computer is easy to picture: common parts are stocked, then configured when the order arrives. A bespoke machine bought and built to order asks for a longer wait. A supermarket item has already been made and positioned in stock. Use familiar examples to make the timing trade-off clear.

## The generic strategy matrix

[diagram:generic]

The operations lecture compares demand predictability with supply lead time. With predictable demand and long lead times, lean planning and optimisation are emphasised. With predictable demand and short lead times, Kanban-style continuous replenishment is suitable. With unpredictable demand and long supply lead times, a hybrid using postponement can help. With unpredictable demand and short lead times, agile quick response is emphasised.

These are design directions, not automatic answers for every item. A product may have predictable base demand and unpredictable peaks. A supplier lead time may be short on average but unreliable. Good analysis uses the actual pattern rather than forcing every situation into a box based on one adjective.

## Push, pull and information

Push means releasing work based on a plan or forecast. Pull links replenishment or production to actual consumption or a downstream signal. A Kanban signal can authorise replenishment, but the system may still use forecasts for capacity and strategic planning. Pull does not mean the business never plans.

Similarly, a decoupling point does not eliminate all upstream information about final demand. Better visibility can improve upstream decisions even where common materials are replenished before a specific order. The issue is the level of commitment and the timing of the decision, not whether actors are allowed to share information.

## Order winners, qualifiers and the reading's cases

An order qualifier is a condition needed to be considered by the customer. An order winner differentiates the chosen offer. Adequate quality might be a qualifier while reliable rapid delivery wins the club's order. Over time, a former winner may become an expected minimum.

The reading's conceptual value relationship combines quality and service against cost and lead time. Treat it as a way to think about trade-offs, not a universal formula into which unrelated measurement units can be inserted to produce a precise score.

The historical computer case discusses reductions in manufacturing and information lead times and the consequences of an assemble-to-order position. It includes a manufacturing lead-time change from about 280 to 150 days and information lead time from about 45 to 8 days. The lesson is that material and information lead times both matter, especially with short product life cycles.

The paper's forecast-error illustrations show uncertainty growing as the forecast horizon extends. Their percentages belong to the historical illustration; do not present them as a general law for every industry. The general managerial implication is to avoid committing to unnecessary product detail before useful demand information becomes available.

### Check your understanding

Why is printing club logos after the order arrives an example of postponement, while waiting to print until after the promised date is not a successful application?

[answer:Possible answer]
The first delays differentiation until the club's actual requirements are known while preserving the delivery promise. The second merely fails to deliver on time. Effective postponement keeps options open and reduces risk within a process capable of meeting D-time.
[/answer]


# Inventory, costs and worked calculations

Inventory is stock held for future use or sale. It can include raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods and maintenance or operating supplies. Inventory helps bridge differences between the timing of supply and demand, but it ties up money and can create storage, damage and obsolescence costs.

Campus Tees holds blank shirts before printing, partly printed batches during processing and finished orders awaiting collection. A bakery holds ingredients, dough in process and finished bread. The same underlying questions apply: why is the stock needed, how much should be ordered, when should replenishment begin and what uncertainty must be protected against?

## Why hold inventory?

Stock can support availability, cover replenishment lead time, separate processes with different schedules and protect against uncertainty. A business may also order in batches because each order or setup has a fixed cost. These reasons should be examined rather than accepted as a permanent justification for every pile of material.

A box of standard blank shirts may allow Campus Tees to respond within the club's D-time. A box of last year's printed event design may have little future value. The physical quantity can be the same while the economic meaning differs. Product variety, life cycle, shelf life and customer requirements matter.

Holding less inventory can release cash and expose process problems. Holding too little can create stockouts and disrupted work. The managerial objective is not the maximum or minimum possible stock in isolation. It is an appropriate system of availability, cost and risk.

## Three independent ways to classify costs

[diagram:costtypes]

The lecture's cost cube separates **fixed versus variable**, **direct versus indirect**, and **engineered versus discretionary**. These are different dimensions. Do not assume every direct cost is variable or every indirect cost is fixed.

A fixed cost does not change with activity within a relevant range and time period. A variable cost changes with activity. Direct costs can be traced economically to a chosen cost object, such as a product or order. Indirect costs are shared and need allocation or another treatment. Engineered costs have a relatively identifiable technical relationship with output; discretionary costs depend more on management's decisions about spending.

For a printed-shirt order, the blank shirts are a direct material cost and generally vary with quantity. A supervisor's salary may be indirect relative to individual orders and fixed within a period. A dedicated machine lease may be direct to one product line while fixed over its relevant range. Marketing expenditure may be discretionary in a way that fabric consumption per shirt is not.

The chosen cost object matters. Rent may be indirect to one shirt but direct to a particular warehouse. State the context if a question asks you to classify a cost. A classification without its basis can be misleading.

### Fixed costs can step up

The lecture's rent chart is a step pattern. Rent remains unchanged across one capacity range, then rises when extra space is required. “Fixed” does not mean unchanged forever at every possible output. It means fixed within the range and period being analysed.

Direct material cost is shown increasing with activity. If each shirt uses one €5 blank and there is no waste or discount, 100 shirts require €500 of blanks and 200 require €1,000. The linear relationship is an assumption of the simple model, not a law that ignores quantity discounts or changing yields.

## Worked calculation: break-even

Let fixed cost F = €1,200, selling price p = €15 per shirt and variable cost v = €9 per shirt. Each sold shirt contributes p − v = €6 toward fixed costs and then profit.

**Revenue = p × q. Total cost = F + v × q. Profit = (p − v) × q − F.**

At break-even, profit is zero. Therefore **qBE = F / (p − v) = 1,200 / 6 = 200 shirts**.

[diagram:breakeven]

At 300 shirts, revenue is €4,500. Variable cost is €2,700 and total cost is €3,900. Profit is €600. At 100 shirts, contribution is €600, which covers only half the fixed cost, so the loss is €600.

| Quantity | Revenue | Variable cost | Total cost | Profit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | €1,500 | €900 | €2,100 | −€600 |
| 200 | €3,000 | €1,800 | €3,000 | €0 |
| 300 | €4,500 | €2,700 | €3,900 | €600 |

If p is equal to or below v, there is no positive finite break-even quantity in this simple model with positive fixed cost. More sales do not generate a positive contribution to cover F. Do not divide by zero or report a negative break-even quantity as a meaningful target.

The model assumes a stable price, constant variable cost per unit and fixed costs within the relevant range. If price falls at high volumes, capacity creates a step cost or unsold output remains in stock, the simple calculation needs adjustment. In an exam, show the formula, substitution, units and interpretation.

[lab:breakeven]

## Two separate inventory decisions

**Order quantity answers “how much?” Reorder point answers “when?”** The EOQ can inform the quantity. The reorder point triggers replenishment early enough to cover lead-time demand and safety stock. Confusing these decisions is a common mistake.

Imagine ordering a new phone charger. Choosing a pack of ten is a quantity decision. Deciding to reorder when only three remain is a timing decision. A business needs both. A perfect order quantity still fails if ordered after stock is exhausted and delivery takes a week.

## Worked calculation: the reorder point

The lecture gives **Reorder point = demand during lead time + safety stock**. With a constant daily demand rate d and lead time L in days, this becomes **ROP = d × L + SS**.

Suppose annual demand is 12,000 units over 300 working days. Daily demand is 12,000/300 = 40 units. Lead time is five working days and safety stock is 60 units. Expected lead-time demand is 40 × 5 = 200. The reorder point is **260 units**.

[diagram:reorder]

Use consistent time units. Multiplying annual demand directly by a five-day lead time is wrong unless you convert the lead time to the same annual basis. A daily demand rate must be paired with a lead time expressed in corresponding days.

With an order quantity of 600, the idealised cycle can start at 660 units, including safety stock. After ten working days at 40 units per day, stock reaches 260 and the order is placed. During the five-day lead time, another 200 units are used, leaving 60. A receipt of 600 raises stock back to 660.

The order cycle is 600/40 = 15 working days. Safety stock is not normally consumed in this ideal average-demand picture; it protects against uncertainty. In practice, review inventory position and outstanding orders to avoid placing duplicate replenishments in more complex systems. The lecture's basic sawtooth remains the first model to understand.

[lab:reorder]

## Safety stock: protection against uncertainty

The glossary describes safety stock as extra inventory held to protect against stockouts caused by demand fluctuations or supply delays. The lecture links it to service level, lead-time variability and demand variability. A higher service ambition or more uncertainty generally requires more protection, all else equal.

Suppose ordinary lead-time demand is 200 but an unusually busy week requires 240. A 60-unit buffer could absorb that increase. If both demand and lead time rise sharply, the same buffer may be insufficient. Safety stock is not a universal guarantee.

Better information can reduce avoidable uncertainty. More reliable lead time can also reduce the required buffer. However, information does not replace physical goods when demand arrives before replenishment is possible. The lecture's memorable statement about replacing inventory with information should be interpreted as a coordination principle, not a claim that data alone fulfils physical demand.

## EOQ: balance ordering and holding cost

The **Economic Order Quantity**, also called the Wilson formula in the glossary, finds an order quantity that minimises the sum of ordering and holding costs under a simple set of assumptions.

Use D for annual demand, K for the fixed cost per order, h for annual holding cost per unit, P for unit purchase price and Q for order quantity. The total annual cost function in the glossary is:

**T(Q) = PD + KD/Q + hQ/2.**

Purchase cost is PD. The number of orders per year is D/Q, so ordering cost is K × D/Q. Average cycle inventory is Q/2, so holding cost is h × Q/2. The model assumes a regular decline from Q to zero followed by an instantaneous receipt of the next lot.

[diagram:eoq]

A larger Q means fewer orders and lower annual ordering cost. It also means higher average stock and higher holding cost. A smaller Q reverses those effects. EOQ balances them. It does not make each cost individually as small as possible.

The optimal quantity is **Q* = √(2DK/h)**. If the purchase price P is constant, PD does not change with Q and therefore does not change the optimum. Quantity discounts require an extended comparison; they are not necessary for the basic EOQ trade-off.

### Worked EOQ example

Let D = 12,000 units/year, K = €30/order and h = €2/unit/year. Then Q* = √(2 × 12,000 × 30 / 2) = √360,000 = **600 units**.

Orders per year = 12,000/600 = 20. Average cycle inventory = 600/2 = 300. Annual ordering cost = 20 × €30 = €600. Annual cycle-stock holding cost = 300 × €2 = €600. Relevant annual cost = €1,200.

If P = €5, annual purchase cost is €60,000 and total annual cost excluding safety-stock holding cost is €61,200. If constant safety stock of 60 is included, its annual holding cost is another €120. That constant addition raises total cost but does not alter the basic EOQ.

| Q | Orders/year | Average cycle stock | Ordering cost/year | Holding cost/year | Relevant total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 300 | 40 | 150 | €1,200 | €300 | €1,500 |
| 600 | 20 | 300 | €600 | €600 | €1,200 |
| 1,200 | 10 | 600 | €300 | €1,200 | €1,500 |

The equality of ordering and cycle-stock holding cost at the optimum is a useful check for the basic model. The curves trade off against each other. Moving away from the optimum in either direction increases their sum in this example.

[lab:eoq]

### Derivation, explained simply

Differentiate T(Q) with respect to Q, treating the other variables as constant. The derivative is **dT/dQ = −DK/Q² + h/2**. At the minimum, set it equal to zero: DK/Q² = h/2. Rearranging gives Q² = 2DK/h and Q* = √(2DK/h).

You do not need advanced calculus to understand the economic idea: each increase in order size saves some ordering effort but adds stockholding cost. The optimum occurs where the marginal saving and marginal extra cost balance. If asked to derive the formula, show the algebra and define the variables.

### Assumptions and limitations

The basic model assumes known stable demand, constant order and holding costs, a constant unit price, no planned shortages and replenishment that arrives as a complete lot. It abstracts from capacity constraints, perishability, minimum order quantities and many practical complications.

A bakery should not order an EOQ of fresh ingredients that spoils before use. Campus Tees should not ignore supplier pack sizes or uncertain product life cycles. The calculation is a useful baseline, and managerial judgment checks whether its assumptions are reasonable.

The glossary says ordering cost falls with increasing order volume due to economies of scale. Read this carefully: in the standard EOQ model, annual ordering cost falls because there are fewer orders, each with a fixed K. A lower purchase price per unit is not part of the basic formula unless explicitly added as a discount.

## ABC classification

ABC classification directs attention toward the items with the greatest economic significance. A common basis is annual usage value: annual quantity multiplied by unit cost. The Pareto-style 80/20 idea is a useful illustration, not a compulsory exact proportion in every inventory.

[diagram:abc]

Suppose five SKUs have annual usage values of €8,000, €800, €600, €400 and €200. Total value is €10,000. The first item is 20% of the item count and 80% of value. It deserves much closer attention than its count alone suggests.

A items normally receive tighter review and control. B items receive intermediate attention. C items can often use simpler controls. Thresholds depend on context, and operational criticality can justify attention to a low-value item. A tiny spare that stops production may need a strong continuity plan despite its low annual spending.

ABC is different from Kraljic. ABC primarily prioritises economic inventory value. Kraljic combines profit impact and supply risk to differentiate purchasing strategy. The two tools can complement one another, but a C item is not automatically routine or safe to ignore.

## FIFO and LIFO: a worked comparison

FIFO means first in, first out. For cost assignment, the oldest costs are assigned to goods sold first. LIFO means last in, first out: the newest costs are assigned first. Keep inventory valuation assumptions distinct from the physical flow of particular units.

Buy ten units at €2 and then ten at €3. Sell ten. Under FIFO, cost of goods sold is €20 and remaining inventory is €30. Under LIFO, cost of goods sold is €30 and remaining inventory is €20. The same twenty units were purchased; the allocation of costs differs.

This example explains the glossary concepts. It does not assert that every accounting framework or jurisdiction permits both methods. If the exam concerns the module's definitions, explain the mechanism rather than introducing unsupported legal claims.

### Check your understanding

If lead time doubles but demand and safety stock are unchanged, does EOQ automatically double?

[answer:Possible answer]
No. The basic EOQ depends on D, K and h. Reorder point rises because expected demand during lead time increases. Quantity and timing are different decisions. In practice, changed lead-time uncertainty may also affect safety stock, but that is another assumption to analyse.
[/answer]


# Replenishment, information and logistics services

Inventory is managed through both physical processes and information. A warehouse can contain the correct goods but still fail if nobody knows where they are or whether they have already been allocated. A system can report stock that does not exist if receipts, movements or losses are not recorded accurately.

This chapter links the glossary's many abbreviations into one understandable picture. Learn what decision each tool supports. Memorising the letters without their role makes it difficult to apply them to a case.

## The information-system map

[diagram:systems]

**ERP**, enterprise resource planning, integrates main business processes, often through shared software and data. **MPS**, the master production schedule, describes the production plan and helps allocate resources. **MRP**, material requirements planning, determines which materials are needed, in what quantities and when. **WMS**, a warehouse management system, supports day-to-day warehouse operations.

For Campus Tees, customer orders and available resources inform the production plan. The plan implies requirements for blank shirts, ink and packaging. Warehouse records show what is already available and where it is located. Procurement and production decisions then become more coordinated.

Do not assume that buying an ERP package automatically creates integration. People need clear definitions, accurate data and appropriate processes. If sales records one size code and the warehouse uses another without a reliable mapping, shared software may spread errors faster rather than remove them.

## MPS and MRP, one step at a time

Suppose Campus Tees plans to produce 300 festival shirts next week. That is a finished-output requirement in its production plan. If each shirt uses one blank, the gross requirement is 300 blanks of the specified sizes. If 80 suitable blanks are available and uncommitted, the net requirement is 220, ignoring other receipts and reservations for simplicity.

If the supplier lead time is five working days, the order must be released sufficiently early for the blanks to be available when production begins. This timing logic is central to MRP: what, how much and when. The example is a simple explanation of the glossary concept, not a full MRP algorithm with every planning parameter.

The MPS concerns what output should be produced and when. MRP translates that plan into component and material requirements. A WMS helps execute warehouse work such as receiving, locating, picking and dispatching the required material. ERP provides broader business integration. These roles can overlap within one software product, but the concepts remain distinguishable.

## SKU, barcode, QR code and RFID

A **SKU**, or stock-keeping unit, identifies a distinct stock item or variant in the business. A small white shirt and a medium white shirt normally need different identities if they are managed separately. The SKU is the identity; a barcode, QR code or RFID tag is a way to carry and capture identifying information.

A barcode uses an optical label that a scanner reads. A QR code is a two-dimensional optical code. RFID uses radio-frequency identification. These technologies can reduce manual entry and support better visibility when the surrounding process records the right events.

The glossary heading “QR – Quick Repsonse” contains a spelling issue and its paragraph discusses QR **codes**. In the agile supply-chain discussion, quick response means a responsive replenishment or supply approach. The two uses should not be collapsed into one definition merely because they share letters.

Scanning a label does not prove the physical quantity is correct. If staff scan one item but move a different one, the record becomes misleading. Good data depends on disciplined receiving, movement, counting and exception handling as well as the technology.

## JIT and Kanban

**Just in time (JIT)** aims to provide what is needed when it is needed, reducing unnecessary stock and improving efficiency. **Kanban** uses cards or other signals to trigger replenishment. A signal authorises the next action based on use or demand rather than an uncontrolled release of extra work.

Imagine two bins of a commonly used packing material. When one becomes empty, a card signals replenishment while the second covers use during the replenishment time. The exact bin sizes and rules must fit demand and lead time. The signal alone cannot make an unreliable supplier reliable.

JIT requires more than frequent orders. Quality, setups, layout, maintenance, supplier coordination and stable information all influence whether small flows work. The lecture explicitly presents in-company tools, inter-company tools and supporting mechanisms. Learn the categories and their connections rather than treating JIT as simply “keep no stock”.

## The lecture's JIT toolkit

| In-company tools | Inter-company tools | Supporting mechanisms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modular designs. | Certified quality. | Quality management. |
| Focus. | Supplier reduction. | Value engineering. |
| Total productive maintenance. | Joint development programmes. | Time-based process mapping. |
| Setup reduction. | JIT delivery. | Six Sigma. |
| Layout and flow. | EDI and internet. | Methods analysis. |
| Pull scheduling. | Integrated transport. | Error proofing. |
| Small machines. | Standard containers. | Management by sight. |
| Lot-size reduction. | Barcoding and RFID. | Enforced problem solving. |
| JIT/MRP. | Long-term contracts. | Under-capacity scheduling. |

**Source:** Inventory lecture, slide 8. The table preserves the lecture's grouping; the explanations below make the mechanisms concrete.

Modular design uses common building blocks to reduce unnecessary variety and support later configuration. Focus narrows the process's task so that resources and methods fit it. Total productive maintenance seeks dependable equipment. Setup reduction makes changing from one job to another less costly, which can make smaller batches practical.

Layout and flow reduce unnecessary movement and interruptions. Pull scheduling limits work based on downstream need. Small machines can provide flexibility compared with a single oversized resource in some contexts. Lot-size reduction lowers the amount released at once, but it needs reliable setups and replenishment to avoid replacing stock with disruption.

Certified quality means building confidence in supplier output rather than repeatedly discovering defects at the receiving point. Joint development helps make products and processes fit one another. Integrated transport and standard containers reduce coordination and handling problems. Long-term contracts can support investments, provided the relationship actually works.

EDI, electronic data interchange, illustrates structured information exchange between organisations. The internet broadens communication possibilities. Barcodes and RFID improve identification and visibility. None of them removes the need for agreed meanings, accurate records and responsibility for exceptions.

Supporting mechanisms help expose and solve problems. Error proofing aims to prevent mistakes or make them immediately visible. Management by sight makes status easy to understand. Under-capacity scheduling reserves some capacity instead of planning every minute at a theoretical maximum, allowing the system to absorb variation and recover.

This last idea connects lean and agility. A system operating at an unrealistic full utilisation can build long queues when anything varies. Some capacity protection may improve flow and delivery. The right amount depends on uncertainty, economics and the required service, rather than a universal percentage.

## Vendor-managed inventory

**VMI** means the vendor monitors and replenishes inventory rather than leaving the buying business to initiate every replenishment. The supplier needs access to relevant stock or consumption information and agreed rules about service, quantities and responsibilities.

Campus Tees could allow its packaging supplier to review stock and replenish standard cartons within agreed limits. The buyer still needs to verify performance and coordinate unusual changes. If the supplier sees only distorted data or does not know about a large event, it can make poor replenishment decisions.

VMI does not by definition determine who owns the stock or when payment occurs. Monitoring and replenishment responsibility are the central glossary points. Ownership arrangements can be agreed separately. Do not automatically equate VMI with consignment inventory.

The potential benefit is better coordination and fewer repeated ordering tasks. Risks include unsuitable replenishment incentives, weak visibility and dependence on the vendor's understanding. A well-designed arrangement makes the shared objective and exceptions clear.

## MRO and operating continuity

The glossary expands MRO as maintenance, repair and operating and describes items used to maintain, repair and operate the inventory management system. More broadly, the term commonly refers to supplies supporting operations. Learn the source wording for this course while understanding why such items matter.

A printer belt, cleaning material or maintenance tool may not become part of the sold shirt, but its absence can stop production. Low direct product cost does not mean low operational significance. This connects MRO management with Kraljic bottleneck risk and safety-stock decisions.

A sensible plan identifies critical spares, lead times, usage uncertainty and alternatives. It need not hold every possible component. The aim is to protect important operations with proportionate cost, information and supplier arrangements.

## 3PL and 4PL

A **third-party logistics provider (3PL)** performs outsourced logistics activities such as warehousing, inventory tracking, packing, shipping or returns. A **fourth-party logistics provider (4PL)** takes a broader coordinating and management role for the end-to-end logistics network, potentially overseeing several providers including 3PLs.

For Campus Tees, using a fulfilment company to store and dispatch finished orders illustrates a 3PL arrangement. Hiring a provider to design and coordinate the wider logistics network, select providers and oversee performance illustrates the 4PL idea. The distinction concerns role and scope rather than simply the size of the provider.

Outsourcing logistics does not remove the customer promise. Campus Tees still depends on correct data, clear responsibilities and the provider's performance. Supplier relationship management remains necessary even when physical logistics work is performed externally.

## Warehouse trends and the information principle

The inventory lecture lists fewer but larger inventories, high automation, data-driven warehouses and real-time analytics. Consolidation can reduce duplicated stock and create scale, but it can also increase distance to some customers or concentrate disruption exposure. A trend is a direction observed in practice, not a requirement that every firm should centralise everything.

Automation can improve speed and consistency where processes and volumes justify it. Data can support allocation, replenishment and exception management. The value depends on how well the information matches the physical system and the decisions being made.

The lecture says, “the only way to replace an inventory is with information.” Read this as a strong emphasis on visibility and coordination. Knowing actual consumption earlier can reduce the buffer needed against uncertainty. It does not mean inventory can always be removed, that data replaces production lead time, or that resilience never needs physical reserves.

## A connected replenishment example

A club confirms 300 shirts. Sales records the specification. The MPS schedules the output. MRP identifies the net material requirement. Purchasing obtains missing blanks. The WMS guides receiving and picking. Scanning confirms movements against SKUs. Production consumes the blanks. Finished shirts enter dispatch. The carrier or 3PL completes the physical delivery, while status information returns to the business and customer.

If the stock file is wrong at the beginning, every later plan may be wrong. If the materials are correct but the club's artwork is late, printing may still miss the schedule. If the finished order is complete but the dispatch data is wrong, delivery can fail. The example shows why information systems support connected processes rather than acting as isolated technical solutions.

### Check your understanding

Does installing RFID automatically make a warehouse agile?

[answer:Possible answer]
No. RFID can improve identification and visibility, but agility also requires market knowledge, responsive decisions and flexible capabilities. Accurate information is useful only if the organisation can act on it. A fast scan cannot solve an impossible production schedule or an unavailable resource.
[/answer]


# Negotiation: reach a workable joint decision

Negotiation is needed when parties must reach a joint decision and have partly different preferences. They depend on one another enough to talk, but they do not begin with complete agreement. A price negotiation, a delivery-date discussion and a conversation about quality responsibilities can all involve negotiation.

The course's practical perspective emphasises understanding the other party's needs while communicating your own. A settlement that one side cannot or will not implement is weak, even if the meeting ends with a signature. This connects negotiation with long-term relationships and the realisation phase after agreement.

## Distributive and integrative negotiation

**Distributive negotiation** treats the relevant value as a fixed pie: more for one party means less for the other. Price can have this structure if all other conditions are fixed. If the buyer pays €1 less, the seller receives €1 less.

**Integrative negotiation** looks for ways to create value by understanding different priorities and combining issues. It is often described as win-win. It is not simply being generous or splitting the difference. The parties search for arrangements that serve their needs better than a one-issue compromise would.

[diagram:negotiationpie]

Campus Tees wants a lower price and reliable supply. The supplier wants predictable volume and fewer last-minute changes. A package with a credible volume commitment, earlier information and staged deliveries may reduce the supplier's cost while improving the buyer's price and continuity. The gain comes from changing the arrangement, not from pretending the parties have identical interests.

A real negotiation can contain both value creation and value distribution. The parties might jointly find an efficient delivery plan and still disagree about how to share the saving. Calling a process integrative does not remove bargaining or the need to protect important interests.

Distributive behaviour is not necessarily dishonest, and integrative language is not proof of fairness. Analyse what issues are being negotiated, what alternatives exist and whether the arrangement is feasible. The course's advice explicitly includes not lying.

## Prepare before bargaining

Preparation means collecting information, understanding needs, ranking priorities, setting objectives and considering the other party's situation. It also means knowing what you will do if no agreement is reached. Entering a meeting without an alternative makes it easier to accept an unsuitable proposal.

The lecture distinguishes three objective levels: the worst acceptable outcome, a fair or realistic outcome, and the best outcome you hope to obtain. These help you evaluate offers without improvising every judgment under pressure. Be clear about which conditions are essential and which can be exchanged.

Campus Tees could prepare a target price, a maximum acceptable total cost, required quality, a latest delivery date and a credible forecast of volume. It should also know whether an alternative supplier is actually qualified. A quoted alternative that cannot meet the deadline is not equivalent to a functioning fallback.

Research the partner's constraints. A supplier might resist lower prices because setup costs are high, but accept a different batch pattern. Asking why a condition matters can reveal possibilities that a sequence of demands would miss. Understanding is useful even when the parties eventually decide not to agree.

## BATNA and the reservation threshold

**BATNA** means the best alternative to a negotiated agreement, associated with Fisher and Ury. It is what you can do if the negotiation does not produce an acceptable deal. A reservation threshold is the point beyond which the proposed agreement is worse than the acceptable alternative, after relevant differences are considered.

These are not identical concepts. “Use Supplier B” is an alternative course of action. “Do not accept a total adjusted cost above €1,650” is a decision threshold. The threshold may be derived from the alternative's price, quality, lead time and risk.

Suppose Supplier B can deliver the required blanks for €1,600 with acceptable quality and a feasible schedule. Supplier A's €1,550 offer may still be worse if it creates €200 of extra handling or unacceptable delivery risk. Compare complete arrangements rather than one headline number.

Do not bluff about an alternative you do not have. The lecture advises honesty. A credible BATNA strengthens the ability to decline a poor agreement; it need not be used as a threat. Sometimes the rational outcome is no agreement, particularly if every available package would leave a party worse off than its alternative.

## Seven phases of the negotiation process

[diagram:phases]

| Phase | Purpose | Practical Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preparations | Gather information, needs, priorities, objectives and alternatives. | Calculate feasible volumes, dates and fallback options. |
| Greeting | Establish contact and a workable atmosphere. | Meet respectfully and allow appropriate introductory conversation. |
| Introduction | Build a shared understanding and agenda. | Clarify the event requirement and issues to resolve. |
| Argumentation | Explain positions and reasons; understand the other side. | Discuss why delivery reliability and predictable volume matter. |
| Compromise | Explore exchanges and packages. | Link price, volume, schedule and delivery frequency. |
| Closure | Confirm the agreement clearly. | Write the specification, dates, responsibilities and price. |
| Realisation | Implement and follow through. | Send forecasts, release orders and review actual delivery. |

The process is a guide, not a promise that every conversation follows seven cleanly separated steps. A misunderstanding during compromise may require more introduction or argumentation. The phases help ensure that important work is not forgotten.

### Greeting and introduction

A useful atmosphere supports communication. Time spent building rapport can have value, especially when the parties expect an ongoing relationship. What feels respectful or efficient can vary across people and cultural contexts.

Introduction establishes the purpose and agenda. Beginning with shared or less controversial issues can help create a foundation. It also clarifies whether the people present have the authority and information needed to decide. A meeting can fail because the actual decision maker was never involved.

### Argumentation

Explain reasons rather than only repeat positions. “We require Friday delivery because the festival opens Saturday morning” is more informative than “Friday is non-negotiable”. The reason helps the supplier evaluate possible methods and alternatives.

Listen actively. Ask questions that reveal underlying needs. Avoid assuming that the first stated position is the full explanation. A request for a higher minimum order may reflect setup economics, transport cost or planning uncertainty, each of which may be addressed differently.

### Compromise and packages

Consider combinations of issues. A lower price may be exchanged for more predictable volume. Faster delivery may require an earlier artwork deadline. A longer contract may justify supplier investment, while the buyer needs suitable performance safeguards.

A package should not hide an essential problem. If the supplier cannot physically meet the required quality, adding an attractive price does not solve the need. The purpose is to find feasible trades, not to conceal incompatibility behind a complex agreement.

### Closure and realisation

Closure should state what was agreed, by whom, when and under what conditions. Written confirmation reduces later misunderstanding. Define specifications, quantities, dates, responsibilities and how exceptions will be handled.

Realisation means doing the agreed work. If Campus Tees promised a forecast every Monday and fails to send it, the negotiated delivery arrangement may stop working. Review performance and learn from the result. Successful implementation also influences actor bonds and the next negotiation.

## Practical advice from the lecture

The lecture emphasises listening, avoiding unnecessary ultimatums, remaining calm, understanding the other side, writing agreements down and never lying. It also offers practical bidding advice, such as letting the other side make the first bid. Treat that as the lecture's guidance rather than a universal claim that no other approach can ever be appropriate.

“Never give more than necessary” does not mean refuse every concession. It means understand the value of what you exchange and link concessions to a purpose. A concession that costs little to you but matters greatly to the other party can support an integrative package.

A threatened deadline or emotional outburst can narrow the conversation before useful options have been explored. Calmness makes it easier to compare an offer with objectives and alternatives. It also helps preserve a relationship when agreement is difficult.

## Intercultural negotiation

The lecture contrasts Swedish and Chinese tendencies using cultural concepts. It describes Swedish negotiation as relatively structured, prepared and oriented toward formal contracts and time discipline. It discusses Chinese negotiation through relationship, respect and concepts such as **guanxi**, **mianzi** and **bao**.

Guanxi concerns relationships and connections. Mianzi concerns face, respect and social standing. Bao concerns reciprocity. These concepts can help a negotiator notice why trust, introductions, respectful disagreement or reciprocal actions may matter. They are not shortcuts for predicting every individual's behaviour.

The lecture uses Hofstede-style dimensions, including individualism, power distance and masculinity, to discuss broad tendencies. Its Swedish illustration has high individualism, low power distance and low masculinity; its Chinese illustration has more collectivism, higher power distance and higher masculinity. These are teaching comparisons, not descriptions of every person or organisation.

A thoughtful response avoids stereotypes. Ask how this particular partner prefers to work, who participates in decisions, how agreement is confirmed and what timing is feasible. An individual may differ substantially from a national average or a classroom illustration.

The lecture also raises whether adapting to the other culture is always beneficial, drawing on work including Brett and Okumura, Francis, Liu and colleagues, and Thompson. The message is not a simple universal rule to imitate the other party completely. Adaptation can be interpreted differently; curiosity, preparation and mutual understanding are safer than mechanical assumptions.

## A full integrative example

Campus Tees initially asks for a 10% price reduction. The supplier initially asks for a six-month commitment. A distributive discussion might settle on 5% without changing anything else. An integrative discussion investigates why each issue matters.

The supplier explains that uncertain order timing causes costly small runs and urgent shipments. Campus Tees explains that it cannot store six months of finished variants and fears being tied to unsuitable quality. They explore a framework agreement with a forecast, agreed release windows, staged deliveries and quality requirements.

The supplier gains predictability. Campus Tees avoids receiving everything at once and gets more dependable supply. The parties still negotiate the price and risk allocation, but the package creates possibilities beyond the original single-number argument. Realisation then tests whether forecasts, releases and quality actually work.

### Check your understanding

Why does “split the difference” not necessarily demonstrate integrative negotiation?

[answer:Possible answer]
It may simply divide a fixed difference on one issue. Integrative negotiation examines underlying priorities and combines issues to create additional value, such as changing order timing to reduce cost for the supplier while improving service for the buyer. The final settlement can still include distributive bargaining over the gains.
[/answer]


# One business, the whole module

This fictional case brings the topics together. It is designed to help you apply the models rather than remember each chapter as an unrelated list. Read the situation, pause to make a recommendation, then compare it with the reasoning below.

## The festival order

A student festival asks Campus Tees for 300 shirts in three weeks. It needs a clear volunteer identity, an attractive design and delivery before the event. Its budget is limited. Final size information will arrive next week, and the logo may still change. Campus Tees has a printing machine, a small warehouse and relationships with two wholesalers.

Wholesaler A is cheaper but sometimes late. Wholesaler B is more dependable and offers better stock information. A specialised printer spare has only one qualified source. The company is also considering outsourcing printing because an external specialist quotes a low unit price.

A good answer should not jump immediately to one tool. Begin with the customer's requirements and the business situation, then use models to examine the connected decisions. The purpose of a framework is to improve the recommendation, not to display every term regardless of relevance.

## Start with marketing and strategy

The club's need is identification and belonging at the event. Its want is a particular shirt design. Demand exists when the agreed specification is backed by an approved budget. This distinction matters because enthusiastic interest without a final budget is not yet a firm production requirement.

The market is organisational: the festival buys shirts to run an event. Demand for blanks and ink is derived from that downstream requirement. Campus Tees should understand the event's timing rather than interpret the purchase as an isolated order for cotton goods.

If Campus Tees targets clubs and positions itself around reliable event delivery, the date becomes central to the offer. A lower purchasing price that makes delivery much less reliable may conflict with the positioning. The target segment and promised benefit should guide the supply design.

The strategy questions are: where is the firm now, where does it want to be and how will it get there? Current constraints include limited capacity, uncertain information and supply risk. The desired outcome is a complete, correct order before the event at an acceptable total cost. The route combines specification control, purchasing, scheduling, postponement and contingency planning.

A resource-based analysis asks what supports the promise. The printer is useful but may be purchasable by rivals. A reliable combination of club knowledge, supplier relationships and scheduling routines might be more difficult to copy. Apply VRIN conditionally rather than declaring the company advantaged because it owns equipment.

## Map the chain and the network

Material flows from upstream manufacturers through wholesalers to Campus Tees and then to the club. Requirements information moves upstream. Availability and shipment information moves in both directions. The club judges the final outcome even if the immediate cause of failure originates several relationships away.

Using ARA, actor bonds include trust between Campus Tees and the wholesalers. Resource ties include the fit between blank-shirt specifications, stock data and the printing method. Activity links include order cutoffs, dispatch, printing and delivery. A change in the final size list affects all three layers.

The direct relationship with Wholesaler A is one analytical level. A's connection to its manufacturer belongs to the recognised small world if Campus Tees understands that dependency. A wider disruption in material supply can affect the relationship even when the focal firm does not see every upstream actor.

This explains why a new contract clause alone may not solve the delivery problem. If the actual constraint is upstream capacity, pressuring the wholesaler for a promise may create an unrealistic commitment. Networking should investigate and change the substance of the activity and resource connections.

## Choose purchasing approaches

The standard blanks might be leverage purchases if several qualified suppliers exist and spending is significant. Competitive comparison is appropriate, but the qualification must include quality and delivery, not only price. Wholesaler B's higher price may be justified by lower total risk and better information.

The specialised spare could be a bottleneck item if its direct profit impact is low but supply risk is high. Campus Tees should investigate a reasonable buffer, maintenance arrangements and alternative qualification. If the spare's business impact is assessed as high because it is central to output, the case may instead justify a strategic classification. State the assessment rather than force the object into a fixed category.

Office supplies are likely routine: simplify their administration. A critical printing platform or specialist capability may need a strategic relationship. This is the Kraljic principle in action: different situations need different managerial attention.

The outsourcing quote should be evaluated against total costs and future capability. Consider artwork transfer, quality checks, urgent changes, transport, coordination and dependence. Also ask whether outsourcing would weaken the knowledge needed to manage the customer promise. The lowest unit quote is not automatically the best make-or-buy decision.

Supplier-base structure offers choices. One qualified supplier can support depth and efficiency but increases dependence. Two qualified sources can provide options but require effort. Parallel sourcing across product lines may combine relationship depth and broader access to capabilities. A second supplier only helps if it can meet the actual requirement in time.

## Design the order fulfilment process

Campus Tees should make the order's information dependencies visible. Artwork approval, size confirmation, blank availability, printing capacity and carrier pickup all need dates and responsibilities. A process map can reveal waiting hidden between those tasks.

If artwork waits in a manager's inbox for two days, buying a faster printer may not solve the lead-time problem. A time-based map can separate useful activity from waiting. A clearer approval process might remove more elapsed time than a small increase in print speed.

The seven wastes provide investigation prompts. Overproduction would be printing speculative club logos. Defects would be an incorrect design. Inventory would include unnecessary finished variants. Motion and transport might result from a poor layout. Overprocessing might be repeated data entry. Waiting could arise from unclear approval. Each proposed improvement should address a real cause.

Quality responsibility should be built into the flow. The artwork agreed with the customer must match the production file. Blank quality must support the print method. Operators need clear standards. A final inspection cannot economically repair every failure created upstream.

## Use postponement and leagility

Final artwork and size information are uncertain, but the event date is fixed. Campus Tees can prepare common resources before the information is complete and delay irreversible customisation. Generic blanks can be stocked or reserved; logos should wait for approval.

This is postponement when it preserves the ability to deliver on time. The CODP occurs where a generic blank becomes linked to the specific order through allocation and printing. Lean upstream replenishment supports the common input, while agile downstream work handles confirmed design and mix.

The firm should compare P-time with D-time. If sourcing plus printing plus delivery takes eight days and the final order allows only three, some upstream work must be prepared in advance or the process must change. A manager cannot solve the mismatch by simply declaring the business “make to order”.

Capacity matters as well as inventory. Enough blanks do not help if the only machine is unavailable. Maintenance, setup planning and reserve capacity can support responsiveness and resilience. The right buffer may be a combination of material, time, information and capacity.

## Apply the calculations

Suppose standard annual blank demand is 12,000, order cost is €30 and annual holding cost is €2 per blank. EOQ gives 600. With 300 working days, daily demand is 40. A five-day lead time and safety stock of 60 produce a reorder point of 260.

These are planning baselines for ordinary demand. A one-off festival order may temporarily change the demand pattern. Campus Tees must incorporate the confirmed event requirement rather than assume the average sawtooth automatically protects every peak. The assumptions behind a calculation matter as much as the arithmetic.

If the event's price is €15 per shirt, variable cost €9 and allocated fixed cost €1,200, break-even is 200 shirts. At 300, the simple model produces €600 profit. A rushed delivery fee, reprint or outsourcing coordination cost would reduce that profit. Use the model to understand the economics, then include relevant changes.

ABC analysis may identify blank shirts as a high-value category deserving close control. The small printer spare may have low annual usage value but high supply risk. This shows why ABC and Kraljic answer different questions and why a low-value item can still require a continuity plan.

## Negotiate a workable package

Campus Tees wants an attractive price, timely delivery and flexibility. The wholesaler wants predictable volume, manageable changes and efficient dispatch.
